subtopics.title: Project Management Information Systems
subtopics.subtitle: Data vs information, MIS/PMIS components, reporting levels, report types and tools

concepts.text: Data are raw, unorganised facts and figures such as daily muster rolls, quantities of cement issued or hours logged by a crane. Information is data that has been processed, organised and put in context so that it is meaningful and useful for a decision, for example 'the concrete work is 12% behind schedule and 5% over budget'. The same item can be information for one person and only data for another, because usefulness depends on the decision being made. An information system is the set of people, procedures and technology that turns data into information and delivers it to decision makers.

rows: Cement use is 8% above estimate this month

concepts.text: A Management Information System (MIS) is an organised system that collects, stores, processes and distributes information to support planning, control and decision making in an organisation. A Project Management Information System (PMIS) is the project-specific version: it gathers schedule, cost, resource, quality, risk and procurement data from the project and produces the reports that the project manager, client and stakeholders need. PMBOK treats the PMIS as part of the enterprise environment that supports every process group, from initiation to closure.

items: Hardware: computers, servers, tablets on site, network and communication equipment.
Software: scheduling, cost control, database, document management and reporting applications.
Data (database): the organised store of project records such as the WBS, activity list, budgets, progress measurements and correspondence.
Procedures: rules and methods for collecting, validating, processing and distributing data, including report formats and frequencies.
People: users and operators, from site engineers entering progress to managers reading reports; the system fails without trained, willing users.

concepts.text: Basic functions of an information system:
items: Data collection (input) from site reports, timesheets, invoices and measurements.
Storage and retrieval of records so they can be found and reused.
Processing: sorting, classifying, calculating, summarising and comparing actual against plan.
Dissemination: delivering the right information to the right person at the right time in the right format.
Feedback and control: variances trigger corrective action, whose results re-enter the system as new data.

rows: Summarised, external, exception and trend reports

concepts.text: Types of reports produced by an MIS/PMIS:
items: Periodic (scheduled) reports: issued at fixed intervals, e.g. weekly progress or monthly cost reports.
Exception reports: produced only when a value crosses a set limit, e.g. an activity slipping beyond its float; they implement management by exception.
Demand (ad hoc) reports: produced on request to answer a specific question.
Status, progress and variance reports: where the project stands, what was done in the period, and how actual differs from plan.
Forecast reports: estimated completion date and estimate at completion based on current performance.

concepts.text: Tools, Quality of Information and Benefits

items: Scheduling and project control software: Microsoft Project, Oracle Primavera P6.
Spreadsheets and databases for estimates, bills of quantities and measurement books.
Collaboration and document management platforms for drawings, RFIs and correspondence.
ERP systems linking procurement, inventory, accounts and payroll to project codes.
Dashboards showing key indicators such as percent complete, CPI and SPI; BIM and GIS for model- and location-based information.

concepts.text: Good information is accurate, timely, relevant, complete, concise and delivered to the person who can act on it. Late or excessive information is almost as harmful as missing information, because managers either act too late or cannot find the key signal. The value of information is the improvement in the expected outcome of a decision made with the information compared with the same decision made without it; information is worth collecting only if that value exceeds its cost.

items: Faster, better-informed decisions and early warning of delays and overruns.
A single, consistent source of project data for all stakeholders.
Reduced paperwork and duplication, and better record keeping for claims, audits and lessons learned.
Improved coordination and communication between client, consultant and contractor.

formulas.plainText: Percent complete = EV / BAC x 100%

formulas.latex: EVPI = EV_{\text{with perfect info}} - EMV_{\text{best without info}}
formulas.plainText: EVPI = expected value with perfect information - best EMV without information
CPI = EV / AC, SPI = EV / PV (dashboard indicators)

notes.text: Match report to level: top management gets summarised and exception reports; operational supervisors get detailed, frequent transaction reports. An exception report appears only when a limit is crossed.
Do not confuse data with information: a figure becomes information only when it is processed and placed in a decision context. Options that describe 'raw facts' describe data.
A PMIS is more than software. Hardware, data, procedures and people are all components, and most PMIS failures come from poor procedures or untrained users rather than from the software itself.

formulas.title: Percent complete
formulas.plainText: Percent complete = EV / BAC x 100%
formulas.description: Share of the total budgeted work actually accomplished, a standard PMIS dashboard figure.

formulas.title: Expected value of perfect information
formulas.latex: EVPI = EV_{\text{with perfect info}} - EMV_{\text{best without info}}
formulas.plainText: EVPI = expected value with perfect information - best EMV without information
formulas.description: Upper limit on what is worth paying for additional information before a decision.

formulas.title: Performance indices
formulas.plainText: CPI = EV / AC, SPI = EV / PV
formulas.description: Cost and schedule efficiency indicators routinely reported by a PMIS; values below 1 signal trouble.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between data and information?
flashcards.back: Data are raw, unprocessed facts; information is data processed and organised in context so that it is meaningful for a decision.

flashcards.front: Name the five components of an MIS/PMIS.
flashcards.back: Hardware, software, data (database), procedures and people.
A report generated only when a monitored value falls outside a preset limit, so managers attend only to deviations (management by exception).

questions.questionText: Which of the following is best described as information rather than data?
options: A list of daily cement issue quantities from the store
Timesheet entries for each labourer on site
A statement that excavation is 10% behind schedule and needs two extra crews
Individual invoice numbers received from suppliers
questions.explanation: Information is processed data placed in a decision context; the schedule statement compares actual with plan and supports action, while the other options are raw records.

questions.questionText: A PMIS report that is generated only when an activity's cost or delay crosses a preset tolerance is called a(n):
questions.explanation: Exception reports are triggered by deviations beyond set limits and support management by exception.

questions.questionText: Detailed, frequent reports on daily material issue and labour attendance are mainly needed at which management level?
questions.explanation: Operational supervisors make day-to-day decisions and need detailed, internal, frequent information; higher levels need summarised reports.

questions.questionText: With perfect information about next season's river flow, a contractor's expected profit would be Rs 50 lakh. Without it, the best alternative has an EMV of Rs 42 lakh. The maximum worth paying for that information is:
questions.explanation: EVPI = expected value with perfect information - best EMV without it = 50 - 42 = Rs 8 lakh.

questions.questionText: A PMIS dashboard shows BAC = Rs 120 lakh, PV = Rs 40 lakh, EV = Rs 30 lakh and AC = Rs 36 lakh. The percent complete of the project is:
questions.explanation: Percent complete = EV/BAC = 30/120 = 25%. PV/BAC (33.3%) is planned completion and EV/AC (83.3%) is the CPI.

subtopics.title: Project Risk Analysis & Management
subtopics.subtitle: Risk process, probability-impact matrix, EMV, decision trees, responses, risk register

concepts.text: Risk, Uncertainty and the Risk Process

A project risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on one or more project objectives such as scope, time, cost or quality. Negative risks are threats and positive risks are opportunities. In the classical distinction, risk is a situation where the possible outcomes and their probabilities can be known or estimated, while uncertainty is a situation where the probabilities cannot be assigned. Risk management aims to increase the probability and impact of opportunities and reduce those of threats.

items: Plan risk management: decide approach, roles, budget, categories and the probability and impact scales.
Identify risks: list risks and their causes and effects in a risk register.
Perform qualitative analysis: rank risks by probability and impact.
Perform quantitative analysis: numerically estimate the combined effect on cost and schedule.
Plan and implement responses, then monitor risks throughout the project.
Brainstorming and expert interviews with the project team and specialists.
Delphi technique: anonymous rounds of expert opinion until the views converge.
Checklists and historical records from similar past projects.
SWOT analysis, assumption and constraint analysis, and root-cause (cause-and-effect) diagrams.
Site investigation and document review of drawings, specifications and contracts.

concepts.text: Qualitative analysis prioritises risks quickly using ratings of probability and impact, often on a 1-5 scale or as very low to very high. Multiplying the two ratings gives a risk score, and the probability-impact matrix places each risk in a red (high), amber (medium) or green (low) zone. High-priority risks go forward to quantitative analysis and response planning, while low risks are placed on a watch list.

concepts.latex: EMV = \sum_{i} p_i \times V_i \quad (\text{threats negative, opportunities positive})
concepts.plainText: EMV = sum of (probability x value) over all outcomes

items: Expected monetary value (EMV): probability-weighted average of outcomes; the sum of threat EMVs is a basis for the contingency reserve.
Decision tree analysis: decision nodes (squares) and chance nodes (circles); EMV is computed from right to left (rolling back) and the branch with the best EMV is chosen.
Sensitivity analysis: vary one uncertain input at a time to see which has most effect on the outcome, displayed as a tornado diagram.
Monte Carlo simulation: sample activity durations or costs from their probability distributions thousands of times to obtain the probability distribution of total cost or completion date.

concepts.text:
Decision: bid for a hydropower tunnel contract (Rs lakh)
Option A - bid high-risk tunnel job
  Good geology  p = 0.6  profit  +50  -> 0.6 x 50  = +30
  Poor geology  p = 0.4  loss    -20  -> 0.4 x -20 = -8
  EMV(A) = 30 - 8 = +22
Option B - bid small road job, certain profit +20 -> EMV(B) = +20
Decision: choose A (EMV 22 > 20), a risk-neutral choice

rows: Change the plan to eliminate the threat
Exploit: make sure the opportunity happens
Shift impact to a third party (insurance, contract clause)
Share: give part to a partner best able to capture it
Acknowledge; keep contingency or do nothing
Accept: take it if it occurs
Refer to a higher authority outside the project

concepts.text: The risk register is the central document of risk management. For each risk it records an ID, description, cause, category, probability, impact, score, owner, response strategy, trigger conditions and current status. Risk monitoring tracks identified risks, watches triggers, identifies new and secondary risks, checks residual risk after responses and uses risk audits and reserve analysis to see whether the remaining contingency is adequate.

formulas.plainText: Risk exposure = probability x impact
EMV = sum of (probability x value)
Contingency reserve = sum of probability x impact over identified threats

notes.text: Insurance, performance bonds and fixed-price subcontracts are TRANSFER. Redesigning to remove the hazard is AVOID. Extra site investigation or a stronger design is MITIGATE. Keeping a contingency reserve is ACCEPT (active acceptance).
In decision trees, subtract losses and costs: a threat's value is negative. Roll back from the right, compute EMV at each chance node, then pick the best branch at each decision node.

Qualitative analysis (probability-impact matrix) ranks risks; quantitative analysis (EMV, decision trees, sensitivity, Monte Carlo) puts numbers on their combined effect. Quantitative work is usually done only for the high-priority risks.

formulas.title: Risk exposure
formulas.plainText: Risk exposure = probability x impact
formulas.description: Expected loss from a single risk, used to rank risks and size reserves.

formulas.title: Expected monetary value
formulas.plainText: EMV = sum of (probability x value)
formulas.description: Probability-weighted value of all outcomes of a decision or chance node.

formulas.title: Contingency reserve
formulas.plainText: Contingency reserve = sum of probability x impact over identified threats
formulas.description: Budget set aside for identified (known-unknown) risks based on their total expected value.

flashcards.front: What are the four classic responses to threats and their opportunity counterparts?
flashcards.back: Avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept for threats; exploit, share, enhance, accept for opportunities (escalate applies to both).

flashcards.front: What does Monte Carlo simulation produce in project risk analysis?
flashcards.back: A probability distribution of total project cost or completion date, obtained by repeatedly sampling activity values from their distributions.
The document listing every identified risk with its cause, probability, impact, score, owner, response and status, updated throughout the project.

questions.questionText: In the classical distinction between risk and uncertainty, a situation is called 'risk' when:
options: The outcome is certain and known in advance
Possible outcomes and their probabilities can be known or estimated
Neither outcomes nor probabilities can be assigned
questions.explanation: Risk involves outcomes whose probabilities can be estimated; under uncertainty probabilities cannot be assigned.

questions.questionText: A contractor may bid for a job with 0.7 probability of profit Rs 40 lakh and 0.3 probability of loss Rs 30 lakh. The EMV of bidding is:
Buying a contractor's all-risk insurance policy for a bridge project is an example of which risk response strategy?
questions.explanation: Insurance shifts the financial impact of the threat to a third party (the insurer), which is risk transfer; the risk itself is not removed.

questions.questionText: Three threats are identified: P = 0.1 with impact Rs 20 lakh, P = 0.3 with impact Rs 10 lakh and P = 0.5 with impact Rs 4 lakh. The contingency reserve based on EMV is:
A tornado diagram is the typical graphical output of which risk analysis technique?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity analysis varies one input at a time and ranks inputs by their effect on the outcome; the bars are displayed as a tornado diagram.

subtopics.title: Project Financing
subtopics.subtitle: Equity, debt, grants and bonds; project vs corporate finance; BOT/BOOT/PPP; WACC

concepts.text: Project financing is the arrangement of funds needed to plan, build and start operating a project. Funds come from owners (equity) or lenders (debt), supplemented by grants, bonds and other instruments. The mix chosen affects the cost of capital, the risk borne by each party and the financial viability of the project.

rows: No fixed return; dividends paid from profit; highest risk and highest expected return
Fixed interest and repayment schedule; interest is tax-deductible; lenders have priority claim
Raise large sums from many investors at a fixed coupon
From government or development partners, usually tied to conditions
Profits ploughed back; no issue cost

items: Internal: retained earnings, depreciation provisions and sale of surplus assets; cheap and without loss of control, but limited in amount.
External: new share issues, bank loans, debentures and bonds, supplier credit, leasing, grants and soft loans; larger in amount but involve issue costs, interest or dilution of control.

rows: A special purpose vehicle (SPV) created for the project
Whole balance sheet of the company
Cash flows of the project alone

items: BOT (Build-Operate-Transfer): private party builds and operates the facility for a concession period, recovering its investment from user charges or tariffs, then transfers it to the government.
BOOT (Build-Own-Operate-Transfer): as BOT but the private party also legally owns the facility during the concession, then transfers it.
BOO (Build-Own-Operate): private party builds, owns and operates permanently; no transfer to the government.
BOLT/BLT (Build-Lease-Transfer) and DBFO (Design-Build-Finance-Operate) are further variants.
PPP (Public-Private Partnership): the umbrella term for long-term contracts in which risks, responsibilities and rewards are shared between government and a private partner.

concepts.text: Capital Structure and Cost of Capital

The debt-equity ratio D/E measures financial leverage. Higher debt raises returns to equity when the project performs well because debt is usually cheaper and its interest is tax-deductible, but it also raises the fixed repayment burden and the risk of default. Lenders therefore require a minimum equity contribution. The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is the average rate the project must pay its financiers and is commonly used as the discount rate or MARR for appraisal.

concepts.latex: WACC = \frac{E}{V} R_e + \frac{D}{V} R_d (1 - T),\quad V = D + E
concepts.plainText: WACC = (E/V) Re + (D/V) Rd (1 - T), V = D + E

concepts.text:
Worked example (Rs crore)
Equity E = 40, cost of equity Re = 15%
Debt   D = 60, interest   Rd = 10%, tax rate T = 25%
V = 100 ; D/E = 60/40 = 1.5 (60:40)
After-tax cost of debt = 10% x (1 - 0.25) = 7.5%
WACC = 0.40 x 15% + 0.60 x 7.5% = 6.0% + 4.5% = 10.5%

In Nepal, public projects are financed mainly through the government budget (revenue and domestic borrowing), together with grants and concessional loans from development partners such as multilateral development banks and bilateral donors. Private participation is encouraged through PPP and concession arrangements under the Public-Private Partnership and Investment Act, 2075 (2019), and many hydropower projects are developed by private promoters under BOOT-type licences with power purchase agreements with the Nepal Electricity Authority. Details and limits are set by the prevailing laws and policies, subject to amendment.

formulas.plainText: WACC = (E/V) Re + (D/V) Rd (1 - T)
Debt-equity ratio = D / E
After-tax cost of debt = Rd (1 - T)

notes.text: BOT and BOOT both end with transfer to the government; BOO never transfers. In BOOT the private party formally owns the asset during the concession, in BOT it typically operates it under concession.

Apply the (1 - T) tax shield only to debt, not to equity: dividends are paid from after-tax profit, whereas interest is deducted before tax. Also compute weights from total capital V = D + E, not from D/E.
Project finance is non-recourse or limited-recourse: lenders look to the SPV's project cash flows and assets for repayment rather than to the sponsors' other assets.

formulas.title: Weighted average cost of capital
formulas.plainText: WACC = (E/V) Re + (D/V) Rd (1 - T)
formulas.description: Average after-tax cost of all capital, often used as the project discount rate.

formulas.title: Debt-equity ratio
formulas.plainText: Debt-equity ratio = D / E
formulas.description: Measures financial leverage; a 70:30 structure gives D/E = 2.33.

formulas.title: After-tax cost of debt
formulas.plainText: After-tax cost of debt = Rd (1 - T)
formulas.description: Interest is tax-deductible, so the effective cost of debt is reduced by the tax rate.

flashcards.front: How does BOOT differ from BOO?
flashcards.back: In BOOT the private party builds, owns and operates the facility for a concession period and then transfers it to government; in BOO it keeps ownership permanently.

flashcards.front: What is meant by non-recourse project finance?
flashcards.back: Loans to a special purpose vehicle repaid only from the project's own cash flows and assets, with no claim on the sponsors' other assets.

flashcards.front: Why is debt usually cheaper than equity?
flashcards.back: Lenders have a fixed, prior claim and bear less risk, and interest is tax-deductible, reducing the effective cost to Rd(1 - T).

questions.questionText: A project is financed with Rs 60 crore equity at 14% and Rs 40 crore debt at 10% interest. With a tax rate of 30%, the WACC is:
questions.explanation: WACC = 0.6 x 14% + 0.4 x 10% x (1 - 0.3) = 8.4% + 2.8% = 11.2%. Ignoring the tax shield gives 12.4%.

questions.questionText: A Rs 500 crore hydropower project is funded with Rs 350 crore of bank loans and the rest as promoters' equity. Its debt-equity ratio is:
questions.explanation: Equity = 500 - 350 = 150; D/E = 350/150 = 2.33 (a 70:30 structure). 0.70 is debt/total capital.

questions.questionText: Under which model does the private developer build, own and operate the facility with no obligation to transfer it to the government?
questions.explanation: BOO (Build-Own-Operate) has no transfer; BOT, BOOT and BLT all end with transfer to the government.

questions.questionText: Which feature distinguishes project finance from corporate finance?
options: Loans are secured on the sponsor company's entire balance sheet
A special purpose vehicle borrows and repays mainly from the project's own cash flows
Only equity is used, never debt
It is used only for small short-term projects
questions.explanation: Project finance uses an SPV with non- or limited-recourse debt serviced from project cash flows, typically for large infrastructure.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an internal source of finance for a construction company undertaking a new project?
options: Term loan from a commercial bank
questions.explanation: Retained earnings are profits generated and kept within the firm; shares, loans and grants come from outside.

subtopics.title: Tender & the Tendering Process
subtopics.subtitle: Procurement methods and bid process under Nepal's Public Procurement Act 2063

concepts.text: Tender and the Legal Framework in Nepal

A tender (bid) is a written offer by a bidder to carry out works, supply goods or provide services at a stated price and on stated conditions, in response to an invitation from the procuring entity. Tendering is the competitive process of inviting, receiving and evaluating such offers to select a contractor fairly and economically. In Nepal, procurement by public entities is governed by the Public Procurement Act, 2063 (2007) and the Public Procurement Regulations, 2064 (2007), with the Public Procurement Monitoring Office (PPMO) issuing standard bidding documents and operating the electronic Government Procurement (e-GP) system.
Objectives of the Public Procurement Act, 2063:
items: Make procurement open, transparent, objective and reliable.
Ensure competition, fairness, honesty, accountability and value for public money.
Give bidders equal opportunity to participate without discrimination.
Enhance the managerial capability of public entities in procurement.

concepts.text: Procurement Methods and Types of Tender

rows: Public notice; any qualified bidder may bid (national or international)
Normal method for larger works and goods
Invitation only to selected, pre-qualified or listed bidders
Specialised work with few capable suppliers
Sealed price quotations from several suppliers
Negotiation with a single supplier without competition
Small value, emergency or sole-source cases, only as permitted

items: Single-stage one-envelope: technical and price offers in one envelope, opened together.

Two-envelope: technical proposal and financial proposal sealed separately; financial proposals are opened only for bidders whose technical proposals qualify. Used for consulting services and complex procurement.
E-bidding: bids submitted and opened electronically through the e-GP system, increasing transparency and reducing bid-box disputes.
The Act also recognises work through users' committees and force account (amanat) under specified conditions. Monetary thresholds for each method are fixed by the Regulations and change by amendment.

concepts.text:
1. Prepare cost estimate and obtain budget approval
2. Prepare bid documents (instructions, qualification and evaluation
   criteria, conditions of contract, specifications, drawings, BOQ)
3. Publish invitation for bids (bid notice) in newspapers / e-GP
4. Sell or issue bid documents to prospective bidders
5. Pre-bid meeting; clarifications and addenda issued to all
6. Bidders submit sealed or electronic bids with bid security
7. Bid opening in public at the stated time; record prepared
8. Evaluation by the evaluation committee; report prepared
9. Letter of intent to the lowest evaluated substantially responsive bid
10. Acceptance, performance security, and signing of the agreement

items: Bid documents: the complete package bidders need to prepare a responsive bid, normally based on PPMO standard bidding documents.

Bid security (earnest money): guarantee submitted with the bid that is forfeited if the bidder withdraws its bid within the validity period, or, if selected, fails to sign the contract or furnish performance security.
Performance security: guarantee furnished by the successful bidder before signing, protecting the employer against non-performance of the contract.
Bid validity period: the period for which the bid remains binding; the bid security must remain valid beyond it.

concepts.text: Bids are opened in the presence of bidders or their representatives who choose to attend, and the bid prices and bid securities are read out and recorded. The evaluation committee first checks each bid for substantial responsiveness (conformity to all essential requirements without material deviation) and bidder qualification, then corrects arithmetic errors and compares evaluated prices. The contract is awarded to the lowest evaluated substantially responsive bid, which is not necessarily the lowest quoted price.

Before acceptance the public entity issues a notice of intention to accept (letter of intent) to the selected bidder and informs other bidders, allowing a short standstill period during which aggrieved bidders may file a complaint as provided in the Act. After that period, the bid is accepted, the bidder furnishes performance security within the stipulated time and signs the contract agreement; failure to do so forfeits the bid security and the next ranked bidder may be considered.

concepts.latex: S = w_t S_t + w_f S_f,\quad S_f = 100 \times \frac{F_{\min}}{F}
concepts.plainText: S = wt St + wf Sf, where Sf = 100 x Fmin / F

formulas.latex: S = w_t S_t + w_f S_f,\quad S_f = 100 \times \frac{F_{\min}}{F}
formulas.plainText: S = wt St + wf Sf, where Sf = 100 x Fmin / F
% above/below estimate = (Bid - Estimate) / Estimate x 100

notes.text: The award goes to the 'lowest evaluated substantially responsive bid', not simply the lowest price. A cheaper bid with a material deviation or an unqualified bidder is rejected.
Do not mix up the two guarantees: bid security accompanies the bid and secures the bidding stage; performance security is furnished by the winner before signing and secures contract performance.

Threshold amounts for sealed quotation, direct procurement and other methods, and percentages for securities, are set by the Public Procurement Regulations, 2064 and are revised by amendment; check the current version before quoting figures.

formulas.title: QCBS combined score
formulas.latex: S = w_t S_t + w_f S_f,\quad S_f = 100 \times \frac{F_{\min}}{F}
formulas.plainText: S = wt St + wf Sf, where Sf = 100 x Fmin / F
formulas.description: Quality and cost based selection score for two-envelope proposals; the lowest price gets a financial score of 100.

formulas.title: Bid variation from estimate
formulas.plainText: % above/below estimate = (Bid - Estimate) / Estimate x 100
formulas.description: Compares a bid price B with the approved cost estimate E; negative values are below estimate.

flashcards.front: Which Acts and Regulations govern public procurement in Nepal?
flashcards.back: The Public Procurement Act, 2063 (2007) and the Public Procurement Regulations, 2064 (2007), with PPMO as the monitoring office.

flashcards.front: What is a two-envelope bidding system?
flashcards.back: Technical and financial proposals are sealed separately; financial envelopes are opened only for bidders whose technical proposals qualify.
If the bidder withdraws its bid during the validity period or, when selected, fails to sign the contract or furnish performance security.

questions.questionText: Under the Public Procurement Act, 2063, a public works contract should be awarded to the bidder who submits the:
options: Lowest quoted bid price regardless of responsiveness
Bid closest to the approved cost estimate
Bid from the most experienced firm
questions.explanation: Award is made to the lowest evaluated substantially responsive bid from a qualified bidder, not merely the lowest quoted price.

questions.questionText: In a QCBS evaluation with weights 0.8 (technical) and 0.2 (financial), a firm scores 90 technically and quotes Rs 50 lakh; the lowest quote is Rs 40 lakh. Its combined score is:
The main purpose of bid security submitted with a tender is to:
options: Guarantee satisfactory completion of the works
Ensure the bidder does not withdraw its bid or refuse to sign if selected
questions.explanation: Bid security protects the procuring entity during the bidding stage; completion and defects are covered by performance security and retention.

questions.questionText: Clarifications given at a pre-bid meeting should be:
options: Recorded and sent in writing to all prospective bidders who obtained the bid documents
Given orally only to bidders who attended
Kept confidential by the evaluation committee
Communicated only to the lowest bidder after opening
questions.explanation: To keep competition fair, pre-bid minutes and any resulting addenda are issued in writing to all bidders who obtained the documents.

questions.questionText: Which sequence of tendering steps is correct?
options: Bid notice, cost estimate, bid opening, pre-bid meeting, agreement
Cost estimate, bid documents, bid notice, pre-bid meeting, bid opening, evaluation, letter of intent, agreement
Bid documents, bid opening, bid notice, evaluation, letter of intent, agreement
Cost estimate, bid notice, evaluation, bid opening, agreement, letter of intent
questions.explanation: The estimate and documents precede the notice; the pre-bid meeting precedes submission and opening; evaluation leads to a letter of intent and then the agreement.

subtopics.title: Contract Management
subtopics.subtitle: Valid contracts, contract types, FIDIC, variations, claims, LDs, retention and disputes

concepts.text: A contract is a legally enforceable agreement between two or more parties that creates mutual rights and obligations. In construction, it binds the employer (client) and the contractor, with an engineer or consultant often administering it on the employer's behalf. Contract management covers everything from award to final closure: administering payments, controlling changes, handling claims and disputes, and ensuring both parties perform their obligations. In Nepal, general contract law is contained in the Muluki Civil Code, 2074 (2017), while public contracts must also follow the Public Procurement Act, 2063.

items: Offer and acceptance: a definite offer accepted unconditionally.
Free consent of the parties, without coercion, fraud, undue influence or misrepresentation.
Competent parties: of legal age, sound mind and not disqualified by law.
Lawful consideration and lawful object: something of value exchanged for a legal purpose.
Certainty and possibility of performance, and intention to create legal relations; written form where the law requires it.

rows: Fixed total price for defined work
Employer bears quantity risk; contractor bears rate risk
Bid as % above/below the estimate's rates
Usually lump-sum for design, supply, construction and commissioning
One contract for design and construction

items: Cost plus percentage fee: fee grows with cost, so the contractor has no incentive to economise; used only in emergencies or undefined work.
Cost plus fixed fee: fee fixed in advance, so the contractor gains nothing by raising cost.
Cost plus incentive fee: target cost and target fee agreed; savings or overruns are shared in an agreed ratio.
Guaranteed maximum price: cost-plus with a ceiling above which the contractor bears cost.

concepts.plainText: Fee = target fee + contractor share x (target cost - actual cost)

concepts.text: A contract document set typically includes the agreement, letter of acceptance, bid, conditions of contract, specifications, drawings and the priced bill of quantities, listed in an order of precedence. General Conditions of Contract (GCC) are standard clauses; Particular or Special Conditions (PCC/SCC) adapt them to the specific project. The International Federation of Consulting Engineers (FIDIC) publishes widely used standard forms: the Red Book for construction designed by the employer, the Yellow Book for plant and design-build, the Silver Book for EPC/turnkey projects and the Green Book short form for smaller works. Development-partner-funded projects in Nepal commonly use FIDIC-based conditions.

items: Variation order: a written instruction from the engineer changing the quantity, quality, sequence or scope of work within the general scope of the contract, valued at contract rates where applicable.

Claim: a contractor's request for additional payment or time due to events such as employer delay, changed site conditions or variations, supported by notice and records within the contractual time limit.
Extension of time (EOT): additional time granted for excusable delays (employer's delay, force majeure, variations) so that liquidated damages are not charged for that period.
Liquidated damages (LD): a pre-agreed amount per day or week of delay payable by the contractor for unexcused late completion, normally subject to a maximum stated in the contract.
Retention money: a percentage withheld from each interim payment, typically half released at substantial completion and the remainder after the defects liability period.

concepts.text:
LD example
Contract price          = Rs 2,00,00,000
LD rate                 = 0.05% of contract price per day
Unexcused delay         = 60 days
LD per day = 0.0005 x 2,00,00,000 = Rs 10,000
LD = 10,000 x 60 = Rs 6,00,000 (check against contract cap)

rows: Expert decides quickly during the works
Binding for now, may be referred onward
Private tribunal chosen by parties (Arbitration Act, 2055 in Nepal)
Final and binding award, limited appeal

concepts.text: Contract closure confirms that all work is complete and accepted, the defects liability period has ended, final measurements and the final bill are agreed, retention and securities are released, claims are settled and records are archived. A completion or taking-over certificate marks handover, and a performance or defects liability certificate marks the end of the contractor's obligations. Lessons learned should be recorded for future contracts.

formulas.plainText: LD = LD rate per day x days of unexcused delay, not exceeding the contract cap
Retention = retention percentage x gross interim payment
Incentive fee = target fee + contractor share x (target cost - actual cost)

notes.text: Item-rate (unit-rate) contracts put quantity risk on the employer and rate risk on the contractor; lump-sum puts both on the contractor. Cost plus percentage fee gives the contractor no incentive to control cost.

Liquidated damages are a genuine pre-estimate of loss fixed in the contract, not a penalty chosen after the event; they apply only to unexcused delay, so any extension of time granted reduces the chargeable days.
FIDIC books: Red = employer's design construction, Yellow = plant and design-build, Silver = EPC/turnkey, Green = short form.

formulas.title: Liquidated damages
formulas.plainText: LD = LD rate per day x days of unexcused delay, not exceeding the cap
formulas.description: Amount deducted from the contractor for late completion not covered by an extension of time.

formulas.title: Retention money
formulas.plainText: Retention = retention percentage x gross interim payment
formulas.description: Sum withheld from each running bill as security for completion and remedying defects.

formulas.title: Cost-plus-incentive fee
formulas.plainText: Fee = target fee + contractor share x (target cost - actual cost)
formulas.description: Contractor's fee rises with cost savings and falls with overruns according to the agreed share ratio.

flashcards.back: A written instruction from the engineer changing the quantity, quality, sequence or scope of work within the general scope of the contract.

flashcards.front: Which FIDIC book is used for EPC/turnkey projects?
flashcards.back: The Silver Book (Conditions of Contract for EPC/Turnkey Projects).

flashcards.front: What is retention money and when is it released?
flashcards.back: A percentage withheld from interim payments, usually released partly at substantial completion and the rest after the defects liability period.

questions.questionText: A Rs 2 crore contract specifies liquidated damages of 0.05% of the contract price per day, capped at 10% of the contract price. Completion is 60 days late with no extension of time. The LD payable is:
questions.explanation: LD per day = 0.0005 x 2,00,00,000 = Rs 10,000; for 60 days = Rs 6,00,000, which is below the Rs 20,00,000 cap.

questions.questionText: A cost-plus-incentive-fee contract has target cost Rs 100 lakh, target fee Rs 10 lakh and a 70:30 owner:contractor share ratio. If actual cost is Rs 90 lakh, the contractor's fee is:
questions.explanation: Saving = 100 - 90 = 10 lakh; contractor's share 30% = 3 lakh; fee = 10 + 3 = Rs 13 lakh.

questions.questionText: Which type of contract gives the contractor the least incentive to control project cost?
questions.explanation: Under cost plus percentage fee, the fee increases as cost increases, so the contractor gains from higher cost.

questions.questionText: A dispute resolution method in which a tribunal chosen by the parties gives a final and binding award, outside the regular courts, is:
questions.explanation: Arbitration yields a binding award (in Nepal under the Arbitration Act, 2055); mediation, conciliation and negotiation rely on voluntary agreement.

questions.questionText: A single contractor is made responsible for design, procurement of equipment, construction and commissioning, handing over a facility ready for operation. This is a(n):
questions.explanation: EPC/turnkey contracts give single-point responsibility for engineering, procurement and construction up to a ready-to-use facility.
